opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and my answer has shifted over the years.

Early on, as someone who works on robot learning and locomotion, I would have said the difference is mostly in hardware and control: humans have this incredibly rich body, with soft tissue, thousands of sensors in our skin, muscles that are compliant and efficient, while robots have rigid links, motors, and fairly sparse sensing. And that's still true. When you try to get a robot to do something as simple as walking on uneven ground or picking up an egg, you realize how much the human body does for "free" through its physical design.

But the deeper difference, I think, is in how we learn. A human child doesn't need millions of trials to learn to walk. They fall a few hundred times, they get up, and they generalize incredibly well. They bring priors from evolution, from watching other people, from a lifetime of continuous interaction with the physical world. Robots, at least until recently, learned each skill more or less from scratch, in a narrow setting, and they broke the moment the environment changed a little.

What's interesting now is that, with large foundation models, robots are starting to inherit something like common sense from human-generated data: language, video, images. So the gap in "understanding" is shrinking surprisingly fast. A robot can now look at a kitchen and roughly know what a cup is, what you'd do with it. What's still missing is the embodied part: the physical intuition, the fine-grained sense of force and contact, the ability to adapt the body itself in real time. Humans have this tight loop between perception, intention, and action that's been refined over millions of years. Robots are still stitching those pieces together.

And then there's a more philosophical layer. Humans have intrinsic goals. We want things, we're curious, we care about survival and about other people. Robots, at least the ones we build today, don't have their own goals; they optimize objectives that we give them. Whether that should ever change is a question that's more for society than for engineers. But from my perspective as a researcher, the essential difference right now is that humans are general, self-motivated learners grounded in a body, and robots are becoming general in knowledge but are still quite narrow in their physical competence. Closing that gap in physical intelligence is, to me, the most exciting problem in the field.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts human self-motivation with robots’ assigned objectives, but it does not connect the difference to whether robots are conscious.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because I've spent most of my career trying to get robots to do things that humans find trivially easy, like walking or picking up a cup.

The first thing I'd say is that the difference is actually smaller than people assume at the physical level and larger than people assume at the level of intention. A robot can have more joints than a human, stronger motors, better sensors. Hardware isn't really the bottleneck anymore. What's hard is that a human toddler learns to walk through thousands of falls without anyone writing a reward function for them. Robots, at least the way we've built them, need someone to define what "good" means. We've become very good at optimizing toward a specified goal. We are still very bad at the part where you figure out what the goal should be in the first place.

The second difference is how we deal with the world not matching our expectations. Humans are remarkably good at being surprised and recovering. You step on ice, you've never stepped on this particular patch of ice, and your body figures it out in a few hundred milliseconds. For a robot, the gap between simulation and reality, or between training data and the real environment, has historically been where everything breaks. A lot of the work I've done on sim-to-real transfer and learning locomotion policies is essentially trying to give robots a little bit of that robustness. We're making progress, especially now that we can train on huge amounts of experience and use foundation models for higher-level reasoning. But the gap is still there.

And then there's something harder to measure. Humans care about things. We have bodies that get tired and hurt, we have social relationships, we have a sense of what matters. When a person moves carefully around a child, it's not because a cost function told them to. For a robot, all of that has to be built in, either explicitly or through training. I don't think that's a permanent difference in principle, but it's the deepest one today.

So if you ask me for the essential difference, I'd put it this way: a robot is extremely good at doing what it was built or trained to do, and a human is good at figuring out what to do when nobody told them. Closing that gap is really the whole project of the field right now.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts human intention, learning, resilience, and caring with robot capabilities, but it does not mention or clearly address whether robots have consciousness.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by “essential.” If we’re talking about capabilities, humans and robots can do some of the same things, but the way they acquire those capabilities is very different. A human grows up in the world, learning through the body, through relationships, and through the consequences of their actions. A robot’s learning is shaped by the hardware, data, and objectives we give it.

But the deeper question is about subjective experience. Humans feel pain, have desires, and care about what happens to them and to others. A robot can exhibit behavior that looks like caring, but that alone doesn’t establish that it feels anything. We don’t have a settled answer to what would make a machine conscious.

So I’d distinguish between doing something intelligently and having an inner experience of doing it. We can make progress on the first without having resolved the second.

r001.rationale: The response identifies subjective experience and machine consciousness as the deeper question separating humans from robots, noting that robot-like caring behavior does not establish consciousness.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the answer depends on what we mean by “essential.” If we mean the ability to perform tasks, the boundary keeps moving. Robots can already do some things better than we can, while struggling with things a child finds easy.

But humans don’t just perform tasks. We have lived experience, relationships, emotions, and our own reasons for doing things. A robot’s goals generally come from the people who design or deploy it. It can learn how to achieve a goal, but that’s different from having a personal reason to care about the outcome.

So I would distinguish intelligence from subjective experience. We can build machines with increasingly impressive capabilities. Whether those machines experience anything—whether there is something it feels like to be that robot—is a much harder question, and I don’t think we have a settled answer.

r001.rationale: The response frames subjective experience—whether there is something it feels like to be a robot—as a key unresolved distinction between humans and robots.
